articles.title: Photos: Thousands march in Haiti in support of Salvadoran troops
articles.excerpt: Thousands of Haitians have taken to the streets of Port-au-Prince to show support for soldiers from El Salvador, deployed by President Nayib Bukele to confront armed gangs that control large sections ...
articles.body_text:
Thousands of Haitians have taken to the streets of Port-au-Prince to show support for soldiers from El Salvador, deployed by President Nayib Bukele to confront armed gangs that control large sections of the capital.

Protesters on Tuesday carried signs reading “Thank you, Bukele” and “Long live Bukele”.

Bukele has sent more than 2,000 troops to Haiti since late October, after four soldiers from El Salvador went missing during an operation by the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF).

The latest Salvadoran deployment, although separate from the GSF, has been welcomed by Haitian authorities, who have long sought additional reinforcements to combat the gangs.

Bukele’s hardline crackdown on gangs in El Salvador has broad public support but has drawn accusations of human rights violations.

On November 10, he claimed to have destroyed the “headquarters” of one of Haiti’s main gangs, releasing video footage of a helicopter attack.

Since then, Salvadoran forces, backed by Haiti’s national police, have taken control of a football stadium in the capital.

On Tuesday, the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights urged all security forces in Haiti to prioritise the protection of civilians and to use lethal force only as a measure of last resort.

In the first 10 months of this year, the UN recorded 4,595 killings and 2,050 injuries linked to armed violence in Haiti.

Haiti, the poorest country in the Americas, has faced a deepening political and security crisis, with gangs tightening their grip on the country through a campaign of violence marked by murder, kidnapping and rape.

articles.title: Ecuadorian fishermen sue Trump administration over drone strike
articles.excerpt:
A group of fishermen from Ecuador have sued the administration of United States President Donald Trump over a drone strike that sank their vessel and injured members of their crew in March.

The lawsu...
articles.body_text:
A group of fishermen from Ecuador have sued the administration of United States President Donald Trump over a drone strike that sank their vessel and injured members of their crew in March.

The lawsuit, filed on Monday in a Pennsylvania federal court, seeks financial restitution and any additional relief the court considers just.

It also petitions the court to issue an order ending the Trump administration’s campaign of strikes targeting alleged drug trafficking boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific.

The complaint centres on the March 17 sinking of the fishing boat La Negra Francisca Duarte II, based in Ecuador.

“We filed the lawsuit because the boat was all we had. Nobody in Ecuador is helping us,” the ship’s captain, Hernan Flores, told the Reuters news agency. “They did all that damage to us, and by the grace of God, we’re alive.”

The government has not claimed responsibility for the strikes on La Negra Francisca Duarte II and two other Ecuadorian vessels that were attacked and sunk in recent months.

A report from the Washington Post in August, however, suggested that the vessels were targeted by the CIA as part of a secret overseas mission.

Other reports have raised the possibility of the attacks being conducted by a US government contractor or a regional ally.

The attacks appear to be similar to an ongoing campaign the US military has claimed credit for.

Since September 2025, the US government has publicly undertaken a series of boat strikes, with the aim of killing alleged “narcoterrorists”.

At least 244 people have been killed as part of that campaign, which experts have described as extrajudicial killing, in violation of international law.

The lawsuit filed on Monday alleges that two drones were launched from a vessel operated by the US in March and proceeded to attack La Negra Francisca Duarte II.

The boat was set ablaze, resulting in “serious burns” for two of the 16 crew members.

“All of the Plaintiffs ended up jumping off the ship and into the sea. They then found their way onto small emergency boats,” the filing said, calling the strike part of an “unprecedented and manifestly unlawful US military campaign”.

After the strike, the crew members say they made their way towards what they believed was a tuna fishing boat nearby but were met by armed men speaking English dressed in military uniforms.

Since Trump returned to the White House in 2025, he has launched a hardline campaign to combat drug trafficking into the US.

That push has coincided with a policy of expanding US military operations across Latin America, often in collaboration with right-wing political allies in the region.

But critics have raised concerns over transparency and potential rights abuses during such operations.

No suspects have been identified in the boat strike campaign undertaken by the US military, for instance, nor has any evidence been presented to the public.

Families, however, have stepped forward to claim the dead as their loved ones. Many have argued that the people killed in the boat strike campaign were not drug traffickers but fishermen and informal workers.

In December 2025, the family of the missing Colombian fisherman Alejandro Carranza filed a complaint about the boat strikes through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, claiming his right to life had been violated.

A few weeks later, in January, the families of two workers from Trinidad and Tobago – Chad Joseph and Rishi Samaroo – filed a wrongful death lawsuit in a US federal court in Massachusetts. The men had reportedly been travelling home from Venezuela after taking work abroad.

But experts say that efforts to hold the US government to account will be difficult, given the lack of transparency surrounding the boat strikes.

The lethal boat strike campaign has continued in recent weeks, with a recent attack taking place on October 27.

The US government has also been involved in non-lethal interception efforts, stopping suspected drug-trafficking boats.

The watchdog group Human Rights Watch said that the US and Ecuador intercepted at least eight vessels between late August and mid-September, on the basis that they were being used to supply drug trafficking groups.

Of the 160 crew members on board those vessels, Human Rights Watch says that 56 were released without charge by court order, 40 were acquitted for lack of evidence, 50 are awaiting trial, and 14 were not formally charged.

articles.title: Whistleblower: Deadly drone strike in Kuwait could’ve been avoided
articles.excerpt: Washington, DC – An American soldier wounded in a deadly Iranian drone attack in Kuwait is accusing senior military officials of ignoring warnings and being ill-equipped ahead of launching the US-Isra...
articles.body_text:
Washington, DC – An American soldier wounded in a deadly Iranian drone attack in Kuwait is accusing senior military officials of ignoring warnings and being ill-equipped ahead of launching the US-Israel war on Iran, according to a whistleblower complaint.

The complaint, obtained by Al Jazeera English on Tuesday, is tied to an Iranian one-way attack drone that evaded air defences at the outpost within the first 48 hours of the war. Six service members were killed, and dozens were injured, including the whistleblower. It remains the deadliest assault on US forces since the war commenced.

The 14-page letter, submitted on Friday to the House and Senate Armed Services committees, alleges that the army repeatedly brushed aside warnings that the Port of Shuaiba in Kuwait was vulnerable to drone attacks. Though the site was fortified, there was no roof.

“The drone threat to the port was raised directly to the commanding general of the 1st Theater Sustainment Command at least three times in the week before hostilities,” the complaint states.

The soldier, who is not named, also alleges the installation had “no physician, no fixed aid station, and only one ambulance”, adding that at least one of those killed “could have survived” if there was adequate medical support on site.

The army says it has completed its investigation of the Port of Shuaiba attack but has not publicly released its findings.

In a news conference following the incident, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth described the drone as a “squirter” that “happened to hit a tactical operations centre that was fortified”.

But senior military leaders have acknowledged that Iran’s Shahed attack drones, known to fly low and slow, have inflicted more damage on the battlefield than anticipated.

Tehran has repeatedly targeted US and allied assets with attack drones and ballistic missiles. As a result, more than 23 American service members have been killed.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the allegations.

articles.title: Pentagon sued by The Intercept, Freedom of the Press Foundation over alleged 'blacklist' of news outlets
articles.excerpt:
An aerial view of the Pentagon building in Arlington, Va., Oct. 22, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

The Pentagon is being sued over an alleged "blacklist" of journalists and new...
articles.body_text:
An aerial view of the Pentagon building in Arlington, Va., Oct. 22, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

The Pentagon is being sued over an alleged "blacklist" of journalists and news outlets maintained by the Trump administration.

The lawsuit, filed Monday by the nonprofit Freedom of the Press Foundation (FPF) and The Intercept in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., stems from a July interaction between The Intercept reporter Nick Turse and the U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) public affairs office regarding Iran's attacks on U.S. bases in the Middle East.

After making repeated phone calls and receiving no answers, Turse was warned by CENTCOM public affairs executive assistant Richard Allee he would be "put on a list of people to disregard" if he didn't stop pursuing the story.

"Turse asked for clarification: 'You have a list of people to disregard?' Allee confirmed with an emphatic: 'Yes,'" the lawsuit states. Turse asked which reporters or outlets were currently on the list. Allee replied, 'I’m not privy to give you that information.' Turse asked if it was a secret list, and Allee stated 'it's not a list that we publicize' before hanging up the phone."

FIRED STARS AND STRIPES STAFFERS SUE PENTAGON, ALLEGE RETALIATION AND FIRST AMENDMENT VIOLATION

The lawsuit alleges that the office of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth ordered staff not to engage with The Intercept reporter Nick Turse. (Octavio Jones/AFP via Getty Images)

Turse later reported in August that he had spoken with an unnamed U.S. official who told him that the office of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth "had a standing order not to engage with" him, according to the lawsuit.

In August, both Turse and FPF filed Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests to seek Pentagon documents pertaining to journalists and news organizations who are on the alleged "blacklist."

CENTCOM has not responded to the requests, according to the lawsuit.

The suit accuses the Pentagon of two counts of "unlawful withholding of agency records by statutory deadline."

PRESS FREEDOM GROUPS THAT BLASTED TRUMP TURN FIRE ON DEM GOVERNOR OVER ALLEGED MEDIA RETALIATION

Lauren Harper, FPF's Ellsberg chair on government secrecy, who filed the FOIA request on the group's behalf, told Fox News Digital allegations of blacklisted reporters "should concern both sides of the political aisle because the tactics that may be used to silence left-leaning outlets today, could be turned on right-leaning ones tomorrow."

"The Pentagon’s budget is at an all-time high, and taxpayers have a right to know how that money is being spent — especially when questions arise about the legality of its operations and potentially dangerous living conditions of its troops," Harper said.

"It is the job of an independent press to ask tough questions about these issues and more, regardless of who is in the White House or who runs the Pentagon."

Turse called the existence of a journalist blacklist "fundamentally un-American."

"The Pentagon is keeping vital information secret from Congress and the public — including the true toll of the Iran War," Turse told Fox News Digital. "The American people have a right to know how many service members and civilians have been injured or killed.

"They also deserve to know the economic costs of the conflict. But the public isn't getting answers because the Pentagon stonewalls and obfuscates. They didn’t want to answer hard questions, so they threatened to blacklist me.

"If they can do it to me, they can do it to other journalists who demand the truth," he added. "This is a disservice to military personnel and the wider public. If the Defense Department won’t come clean about the war, we’ll compel them in court."

NEW YORK TIMES BLASTS ‘ABUSIVE’ TRUMP SUBPOENAS TARGETING REPORTERS’ SOURCES

The Intercept reporter Nick Turse questioned CENTCOM about Iran's attacks on U.S. bases in the Middle East. (Fox News)

CENTCOM previously denied having a blacklist and called Turse’s account "a complete misrepresentation of exchanges that occurred." It also accused him of repeatedly harassing its staff.

A spokesperson for the Pentagon declined to comment to Fox News Digital. The Intercept did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Joseph A. Wulfsohn is a media reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to joseph.wulfsohn@fox.com and on Twitter: @JosephWulfsohn.

articles.title: Pentagon detains senior US Army officer accused of spying for Russians after UK arrest
articles.excerpt: Fox News' Gillian Turner reports on a senior U.S. Army officer detained in Britain over suspected Russian espionage. Authorities are searching two locations as U.S. officials warn about insider threat...
articles.body_text:
Fox News' Gillian Turner reports on a senior U.S. Army officer detained in Britain over suspected Russian espionage. Authorities are searching two locations as U.S. officials warn about insider threats.

A U.S. Army lieutenant colonel suspected of spying for Russia was handed over to U.S. military authorities Tuesday, days after British counterterrorism police arrested him on suspicion of violating national security laws.

Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, 41, was arrested Nov. 10 near Gloucester, England, on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service and obtaining or disclosing protected information under the United Kingdom's National Security Act.

British authorities previously said the allegations involved Russia, which the Kremlin denied any connection to.

SENIOR US ARMY SOLDIER ARRESTED IN UK ON SUSPICION OF SPYING FOR RUSSIA

A U.S. Army lieutenant colonel suspected of spying for Russia was handed over to U.S. military authorities Tuesday. (Sarah Crabill/Getty Images, File)

The Associated Press, citing a U.S. official, reported that Tyner had not provided information to Russia.

Tyner's transfer followed consultations between British prosecutors, the U.K. attorney general's office and U.S. authorities, according to London's Metropolitan Police.

Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of U.K.'s Counter Terrorism Policing, said investigators referred the case to the Crown Prosecution Service, which consulted the attorney general's office and U.S. authorities before transferring the investigation.

RUSSIAN SPIES ORCHESTRATED $40K MURDER PLOT IN NATION’S CAPITAL, US ALLEGES

Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, 41, was arrested by British authorities Nov. 10 near Gloucester, England. (Jacob King/PA Images via Getty Images, File)

"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," Taylor said in a statement.

FBI Director Kash Patel said the officer was in custody following a joint espionage investigation involving the FBI's Philadelphia field office, its London legal attaché office, British counterterrorism police, MI5, U.K. defense counterintelligence officials and U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command.

"This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk. That’s been demonstrated by the 167 counterintelligence and espionage arrests we’ve made over the last 21 months, a 53% increase," Patel said.

FBI Director Kash Patel said Tyner was in custody following a joint espionage investigation. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images, File)

Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commander of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, warned service members against violating their oath to defend the Constitution.

"This case should serve as a stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath we all take to protect and defend the Constitution," Stinchon said.

Tyner was handed over to U.S. military authorities Tuesday. (J. David Ake/Getty Images, File)

Tyner, who previously deployed to Afghanistan, Iraq and Qatar, served as a senior human resources officer with NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps at Imjin Barracks near Gloucester.

The British-led multinational force, which includes personnel from 20 nations, is designed to respond rapidly to military crises and operations.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov denied Russian involvement following Tyner's arrest, according to the AP.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has denied Russian involvement following Tyner's arrest, according to the AP. (Sputnik/Sergey Guneev/Kremlin via Reuters, File)

"This arrest does not concern us in any way," Peskov said Nov. 11. "We don’t know what it’s connected to. We have nothing to do with this."

British police said Tyner's arrest was unrelated to other ongoing counterterrorism investigations.

According to a Nov. 13 statement from the U.S. Army, Tyner entered active-duty service in January 2008 and deployed to Afghanistan from December 2013 to December 2014, Qatar from July 2016 to July 2017, and Iraq from December 2019 to July 2020.

articles.title: Kuwait reports drone attacks as Iran, US trade attacks on Qeshm and Bahrain
articles.excerpt:
Kuwait’s army has said the Gulf country is under attack by drones while the United States and Iran traded blows, marking escalating tensions in the region as a peace deal remains elusive.

The militar...
articles.body_text:
Kuwait’s army has said the Gulf country is under attack by drones while the United States and Iran traded blows, marking escalating tensions in the region as a peace deal remains elusive.

The military said in a statement on X on Tuesday that “any explosion sounds heard are the result of air defence systems intercepting hostile attacks”.

The US earlier carried out several attacks on Iran’s southern island of Qeshm, in the Strait of Hormuz, hours after Iran said it launched a drone attack on a US radar system in Bahrain.

“The American attack on locations on Qeshm island caused no damage to residential, commercial, or infrastructural areas,” Ahmad Nafisi, deputy governor of Iran’s southern Hormozgan province, told the official IRNA news agency on Tuesday.

He said the situation was under control and relief agencies were on full alert. IRNA reported five to six explosions on the island on Tuesday evening.

A US official told Al Jazeera the strike hit a missile launch site on Qeshm, in response to Iran’s earlier attack on a US base in Bahrain.

US Central Command said Iranian drones aimed at a US radar system at an air base in Bahrain “were intercepted without any damage to US equipment or personnel”.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it carried out a “precision operation” with drones on the US-operated radar at the Sheikh Isa air base, in response to “repeated violations of Iranian airspace by US military drones”.

Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet, said its air defences intercepted the attack, and blasts were heard over the capital, Manama, according to the AFP news agency.

It was the third Iranian drone attack on Bahrain in five days after a lull of several weeks. Friday’s strike was the first Iranian attack on a Gulf country since early September, AFP reported. Reuters said it came after a Bahraini court sentenced 64 people, mostly Shia clerics, to life in prison for allegedly colluding with Iran.

Kuwait’s armed forces said on Tuesday night that its air defences were responding to “hostile drone attacks” and urged the public to follow safety instructions.

It did not say where the drones came from or whether there were casualties or damage.

Iran’s armed forces said three oil tankers struck naval mines while trying to cross the strait on Tuesday. The US military says it cleared the main routes of mines.

Since the war began on February 28, Iran has tried to restrict traffic through the strait, which normally carries about a fifth of the world’s oil, insisting that ships use only routes it has authorised. The US has responded with a naval blockade of Iranian ports and has escorted tankers.

Another tanker, the Panamanian-flagged Tara Gas, was struck on Monday about seven nautical miles north of Khasab, in Oman, causing a fire in its engine room, according to the security firm Vanguard.

Vanguard and India’s ports minister initially said all 25 crew, 24 of them Indian, were safe. But the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said the vessel was hit a second time and the crew were “currently unaccounted for”. India’s ports minister later said the crew had abandoned the vessel after a second attack and that one Indian sailor was missing. Another Panamanian-flagged tanker, the On Phoenix, was hit by an unidentified projectile off Oman’s coast on Monday.

Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and his Omani counterpart, Badr Albusaidi, discussed safeguarding shipping and diplomatic options in Muscat, Oman’s news agencies said.

A third US aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, arrived in the Middle East on Monday, and US President Donald Trump is due to hold a three-way summit on Thursday in China with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, where the Iran war is on the agenda.

articles.title: Sleeve checks and no smartglasses: South Korea races to protect all-important university exams against AI
articles.excerpt:
South Korea has been gripped by revelations of AI-aided cheating, just days before more than half a million students are to sit high-stakes entrance exams

The integrity of South Korea’s career-defini...
articles.body_text:
South Korea has been gripped by revelations of AI-aided cheating, just days before more than half a million students are to sit high-stakes entrance exams

The integrity of South Korea’s career-defining university entrance exam has been thrown into doubt after the top scorer in a recent professional exam admitted using a concealed camera and AI to cheat.

On Thursday, more than half a million people, mostly school students, are due to sit the exam, known as the suneung, at 1,312 centres across the country. The exam runs for a gruelling eight hours over a single day and determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects.

The country goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft take-offs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended.

The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre. Extra trains run from 6am, police drive latecomers to their exam halls, and tourist attractions open late to ease traffic. Offices are asked to open at 10am.

But in recent days, exam organisers have faced a renewed threat to the validity of the entire exercise, after the top scorer in this year’s tax accountancy exam- who got just one question wrong out of 160– admitted on Sunday he had cheated by using AI.

Prime minister Han Seong-sook told a cabinet meeting in Seoul on Tuesday that AI-assisted cheating was a “social evil” that the government would “root out”.

“We will block outright the carrying of smart devices during the exam,” she said. The education ministry and other agencies should approach it “as if staking their jobs on it”, she added.

Han said smart devices must be turned off and handed in, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials would also inspect all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars, sleeves and buttons for concealed cameras.

The government will also send emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sound at full volume and cannot be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who has not handed in their device.

More invigilators will be deployed, and the government said it was preparing to switch off school wifi inside exam centres and public wifi nearby, and that personal hotspots, which cannot be blocked, would be traced through connection records.

The weekend’s cheating revelation captured national headlines in South Korea, stoking concern about the security of the suneung.

In a video posted to his lawyer’s YouTube channel, the exam cheat said he had photographed the questions with a concealed microcamera, sent them to an AI system and read the answers from a smartphone. “I cheated in the tax accountant exam,” he said. “My top placing is not the result of legitimate effort.”

His lawyer handed police a camera, a laptop and a phone. No charges have been brought, and the prime minister has ordered procedures to begin that would void his result and bar him for five years.

The education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, told parliament on Monday that while authorities could screen out the smart glasses already on sale at Thursday’s exam, newer variants could not be dealt with perfectly.

Choi has ruled out postponing the exam, which has been delayed several times before, including in 2017, after an earthquake struck the south-eastern city of Pohang, and in 2020 due to the Covid pandemic.

Smart glasses have been banned in exams since the end of June. In October, several candidates were caught with them while sitting university-run admissions exams. At the suneung, wearing a pair counts as using one even when switched off.

The education ministry looked at using radio-frequency equipment to detect the glasses in exam halls, but concluded conditions varied too much between venues for deployment this year. Checks will instead rely on visual inspection, with at least one dedicated official placed in each exam centre.

Teachers’ unions have criticised the government response as belated. A survey last month of 2,716 secondary school teachers by the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union showed that 82.3% said they could not tell whether a candidate was wearing smart glasses under the current procedure, with only 3.5% saying they could.

To avoid facing scrutiny on exam day, some candidates are reportedly switching to contact lenses. An optician in Suwon, south of Seoul, said students who had never worn contacts were coming in to ask how to put them in.

Han said on X on Monday that the checks would be handled carefully “so that candidates acting in good faith do not suffer unnecessary anxiety or inconvenience”.

In his video confession, the accountancy test cheat addressed suneung candidates directly. “The suneung is coming up soon,” he said.

“To anyone thinking of cheating as I did: I am going to tell the investigators everything, so please don’t think, ‘I won’t get caught.’”

articles.title: New lawsuit alleges AI app 'Bron' used LeBron James’ tattoos, voice and jersey to promote sports-betting tool
articles.excerpt: The Philadelphia 76ers beat the Detroit Pistons, and LeBron James has taken a playmaker role. Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, and Kevin Wildes ask if the 76ers can make the NBA Finals, and if the Kansas...
articles.body_text:
The Philadelphia 76ers beat the Detroit Pistons, and LeBron James has taken a playmaker role. Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, and Kevin Wildes ask if the 76ers can make the NBA Finals, and if the Kansas City Chiefs should trade for George Pickens.

LeBron James filed a lawsuit Tuesday against the developers of an AI sports-betting app, accusing the company of violating his publicity rights and trademarks by branding the product "Bron" and using AI-generated images of him in marketing materials.

The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in New York, claims the developers used James’ name, likeness and nickname without permission to promote an otherwise unknown product. James’ attorneys described the alleged conduct as "a willful, bad-faith tactic" designed to capitalize on the 76ers star’s fame.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

The complaint asks the court to bar the developers from using James’ name, surrender any resulting profits and pay damages, including the fair-market value of its alleged use and punitive damages.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

LeBron James #23 of the Philadelphia 76ers looks on during the game against the Chicago Bulls on November 2, 2026 at Xfinity Mobile Arena in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. NBAE (Photo by David Dow/NBAE via Getty Images) (David Dow/NBAE via Getty Images)

"Defendants did not care that they had engaged in illegal conduct to gain notoriety for their previously unknown app," the lawsuit read. "They intentionally created the false impression that Mr. James endorsed and was affiliated with their Bron App, in an effort to drive downloads and paid subscriptions."

PlayVision Inc., the California-based developer of the app, was launched in 2025 by CEO Anish Gupta and CTO Marc Zoghby with backing from startup accelerator Y Combinator. The company developed a platform that uses artificial intelligence to analyze game and practice footage for sports teams and fans.

LEBRON JAMES SENDS CEASE AND DESIST TO 'BRON AI' SPORTS BETTING APP OVER UNAUTHORIZED LIKENESS

PlayVision launched the "Bron" app this year, saying it does not accept wagers directly but charges a subscription fee for features such as bet tracking and odds comparisons. A marketing campaign this month depicted a person resembling James, complete with similar tattoos, voice and No. 23 jersey, using the app in a locker room.

Messages sent by OutKick through the app’s website seeking comment were not immediately returned Tuesday.

Philadelphia 76ers forward LeBron James looks on against the Indiana Pacers at Xfinity Mobile Arena on Nov. 15, 2026, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Mitchell Leff/Getty Images)

A spokesperson for James previously confirmed that his lawyers sent the company a cease-and-desist letter. PlayVision removed the ad, but not before it was reposted and viewed roughly 1 million times, according to the lawsuit.

"I’m sure the intent here was for us to send a cease and desist in order to make it a story," James' longtime media advisor Adam Mendelsohn told Front Office Sports. "You would prefer not to respond but you don’t have a choice in a situation like this. It’s not the first time and it won’t be the last. For what it’s worth, these gimmicks never work because people see through it."

LEBRON JAMES SAYS 'MY FAMILY IS SAFE' AFTER MAN CAUGHT ON GROUNDS OF HIS LOS ANGELES HOME

Gupta responded to the attorneys’ demand on social media by writing that the app would get a new name, but no new name had been adopted by the time the lawsuit was filed, leading James’ legal team to suggest the company was milking the controversy for attention. Gupta wrote on social media this week that the new name will be announced Wednesday.

Los Angeles Lakers forward LeBron James holds the ball during a timeout in the third quarter. The Boston Celtics played the Lakers at TD Garden on Dec. 5, 2025. (Barry Chin/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)

The lawsuit notes that James typically commands tens of millions of dollars for such endorsement deals, and that he already has an exclusive deal with the prediction market platform Polymarket. It alleges that the app’s marketing was especially harmful in part because it showed the AI-generated James scrolling through bets involving NBA players.

James left the Los Angeles Lakers after eight seasons this offseason and joined the Philadelphia 76ers. Through 15 games of the 2026-27 season, Philadelphia’s 12 wins lead the Eastern Conference. James’ former team also has 12 wins and is tied with the San Antonio Spurs atop the Western Conference.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Chantz Martin is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

Ring of Honor star Deonna Purrazzo talks to OutKick about the notion that independent wrestling is dying.

Deonna Purrazzo is the Ring of Honor women’s pure champion and she’s been able to help put on two successful independent professional wrestling shows this year alone.

Purrazzo, with her pro wrestling star husband Steve Maclin, put on Battle for the Brave and JTown Smackdown. The former helped Tunnel 2 Towers earlier this year and the latter put the need for funding in a New Jersey school district in the spotlight. All was done while social media debated whether independent wrestling was dead or dying.

Former Jefferson High School cheerleader turned pro wrestler Deonna Purrazzo speaks at a rally at Jefferson Township High School to urge Trenton to grant impact aid to a school system facing a $4.8 million deficit, which school officials blame on the state funding formula and development restrictions in the Highlands Region. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

OutKick Dropkick asked Purrazzo before JTown Smackdown occurred last weekend whether she believed the indies were dead or dying.

"I think they're wrong. I think they're so wrong. … The one thing that Steve and I have learned through Battle for the Brave, through JTown Smackdown, is how to balance a budget and how not to over strive and overproduce a show," she said. "All of these things that we're doing, all the proceeds go to really great organizations and really great causes.

"If we overspend someone else's money, then there's no profit in the end for the children of Jefferson Township, for our first responders and our veterans and their families. So, I think that it's all about how you balance a budget, but also how you serve the audience to the best of your ability."

Deonna Purrazzo makes her way to the ring during AEW Collision on June 15 at the Covelli Centre in Youngstown, Ohio. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Purrazzo added that there were plenty of independent wrestling shows happening across the U.S. every weekend. On almost any given day, a promotion is hosting a show. Sometimes, they are hard to find, but it’s even tougher to beat the entertainment being given out at reasonable prices.

Plus, you may see a star or two in the making. Over the last two weekends, in New Jersey alone, the future of women’s professional wrestling was on display. Purrazzo herself is a major star in Ring of Honor, while Maclin was a champion at Total Nonstop Action Wrestling (TNA) and had a banger match with Adam Copeland at Maple Leaf Pro’s Northern Rising in Canada.

"I don't think independents are dead," Purrazzo continued. "If you look across all of professional wrestling, there are dozens of shows every Thursday, every Friday, every Saturday, giving wrestlers the opportunity to get in front of an audience and to maximize their social media.

"I mean, there's always going to be controversy as companies pull back or scale down or cancel shows, but at the end of the day, it's the people who are in it, who are living it, who are immersed in it that know that that's not true."

While the rest of college football try and figure out how put together the perfect schedule, Dakich says Curt Cignetti has already mastered the art of scheduling.

The Mahomes roster is growing, and Patrick and Brittany are having a boy.

Kansas City's royal family made the official announcement on Tuesday with a blue-frosting cake reveal on Instagram, granting the Chiefs quarterback's wish from last week's podium.

The biggest problem for the rest of the league is that Brittany Mahomes is 3-for-3 on Super Bowl runs while pregnant. Every single time.

BRITTANY MAHOMES IS PREGNANT AGAIN, SO IT'S TIME TO BUY A CHIEFS AFC FUTURES BET

Sterling arrived right after Super Bowl LV. Bronze showed up during the 2022 championship run. Golden landed weeks before Super Bowl LIX.

Patrick joked last week about keeping the streak rolling, though he wisely admitted he wasn't sure Brittany had signed off on that plan.

Patrick Mahomes and Brittany Mahomes attend the 2024 TIME100 Gala at Jazz at Lincoln Center in New York City on April 25, 2024. (Kristina Bumphrey/Variety)

Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes (15) throws a pass during the second half against the Los Angeles Chargers at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium on Dec. 14, 2025. (Jay Biggerstaff/Imagn Images)

Even before Tuesday's reveal, Mahomes was already on an absolute heater. Two days earlier, Mahomes shook off a minor elbow scare to dismantle Atlanta's defense, torching the Falcons for 348 yards and five touchdowns in a 35-13 rout.

Eleven months removed from a torn ACL, the three-time Super Bowl MVP is firing on all cylinders again.

PATRICK MAHOMES WORRIED ABOUT SORE ARM THEN THREW 5 TDS; 49ERS' ROCKY MOUNTAIN HIGH; JORDAN LOVE HATES SACKS

Patrick Mahomes of the Kansas City Chiefs talks with his wife Brittany Mahomes prior to the game against the Washington Commanders at Arrowhead Stadium on Oct. 27, 2025, in Kansas City, Missouri. (Jamie Squire/Getty Images)

Better yet, Mahomes looked reporters dead in the eye in July 2024 while expecting Golden and swore, "I'm done. I did three and I'm done."

But that "retirement" lasted about as long as Tom Brady's. Mahomes had campaigned for a second son, so Bronze wouldn't be outnumbered, and he finally got his wish.

Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes and wife Brittany pose for a photo on the red carpet at the Nelson Art Gallery on Jun 13, 2024 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Denny Medley/USA TODAY Sports)

Most guys with half a billion dollars and three rings would be kicking back on a beach.

The 31-year-old future Hall of Famer is clearly wired differently.

articles.title: Tag team: dual waterspouts appear in San Francisco Bay amid stormy weather
articles.excerpt:
Phenomenon is not a common occurrence in the Bay area and inclement weather is expected to continue for few days

A pair of waterspouts were recorded recently in the San Francisco Bay area, much to th...
articles.body_text:
Phenomenon is not a common occurrence in the Bay area and inclement weather is expected to continue for few days

A pair of waterspouts were recorded recently in the San Francisco Bay area, much to the delight and shock of several observers, as storms pummelled the region.

Two waterspouts – vortexes of air and water mist, essentially tornadoes – cut a sheer streak into the sky, as they spiraled above the bay, according to social media footage capturing the weather phenomenon.

While prevalent in the Great Lakes and the south-east Floridian coast, waterspout sightings are not common for the Bay area, according to federal storm data.

The National Weather Service (NWS) confirmed the waterspout occurrence in a Monday special marine warning. Some waterspouts, dubbed “fair weather”, are weak, while others, typically tornadic waterspouts can pose a risk to boaters and coastal areas if they travel on shore.

The inclement weather is set to continue for a few more days. According to an NWS forecast, the Bay area is predicted to be drenched in rain on Tuesday with potential thunderstorms on Wednesday and Thursday.

Elevated tide levels raise the risk of coastal flooding through at least Thursday, according to the agency.

Powerful wind is also forecasted with East Bay Hills expected to see gusts reaching up to 70mph (112 km/h).

After Thursday evening, the showers may subside with some rain lingering over the Pacific and its adjacent inland communities.

articles.title: Pope Leo breaks silence on rosary striking his face in Peru, reveals details about cancer: 'Major surgery'
articles.excerpt:
Video captures the moment prayer beads hit Pope Leo near his eye as he rode through Lima in the popemobile. (Credit: Reuters)

Pope Leo XIV broke his silence Monday after being struck in the face by a...
articles.body_text:
Video captures the moment prayer beads hit Pope Leo near his eye as he rode through Lima in the popemobile. (Credit: Reuters)

Pope Leo XIV broke his silence Monday after being struck in the face by a rosary thrown by a worshipper in Peru, joking about the incident while also revealing details for the very first time about his cancer diagnosis and major surgery which took place before his recent trip to South America.

The pope, who had the lower lobe of his right lung removed Oct. 13, after doctors found a cancerous tumor, told reporters on the flight home to Rome that he has not fully recovered, but said he was determined to complete the long-planned 12-day journey.

"Just over a month ago, as everybody knows, I underwent rather major surgery," Leo, 71, said during a roughly 45-minute news conference on board the papal plane returning from Lima, Peru.

POPE LEO WELCOMED BACK AS HE DELIVERS ANGELUS PRAYER DAYS AFTER LUNG CANCER SURGERY

Pope Leo XIV, flanked by Director of the Holy See Press Office Matteo Bruni, meets with journalists on the return flight from Latin America, Monday, in Lima, Peru. (Elisabetta Trevisan/Vatican Media via Vatican Pool/Getty Images)

"But from the very beginning, I had in mind that this trip had been planned and that I was going to make it happen."

The pontiff credited his recovery to prayer, medical care and personal determination.

"So, with God's help — and I firmly believe in the power of prayer, as I have literally received messages from all over the world — together with a certain personal determination, which I also have, and with the help of the doctors, it proved to be possible."

Despite the demanding itinerary that included multiple flights and appearances before massive crowds in Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, Leo acknowledged that he is still regaining his strength.

POPE LEO XIV SEEN FOR FIRST TIME SINCE LUNG CANCER SURGERY AMID MAJOR RECOVERY MILESTONE

Pope Leo's 12-day tour began in Uruguay and went through Argentina before ending in Peru. (Andrew Medichini/AP Photo)

"I must say that I am not at 100%, but I am doing quite well. Stamina is a gift I have received from the Lord," he said.

The pope also revealed that his cancer diagnosis came as a shock after doctors found an abnormality during a routine annual medical examination.

"The initial news came as a surprise. There were no symptoms — I felt fine," he said.

"It was discovered during some medical tests, as part of what you might call a check-up: a routine annual examination that I have been having for many years."

Leo said the abnormality initially appeared as a shadow on his lung before additional testing revealed a tumor.

POPE LEO UNDERGOES BLOOD TESTS, X-RAY FOLLOWING CANCER SURGERY, VATICAN SAYS

Pope Leo XIV addresses the media aboard the flight from Lima to Rome.  (Simone Risoluti/Vatican Media via Vatican Pool/Getty Images)

"A biopsy then confirmed that it was a tumor," he said, before adding that he had decided to get it done "right away."

"By the grace of God, I remained calm," he added.

The surgery removed the lower lobe of his right lung after doctors diagnosed lung adenocarcinoma, a type of lung cancer. The pope was discharged four days later.

"No further treatment is necessary. However, as a precaution, I will need to continue having these routine check-ups, simply to keep an eye on things, as is normal," he explained.

The Vatican cleared the pontiff to move forward with his South American trip after medical evaluations in late October.

The journey, which began Nov. 6, marked Leo's first papal visit to Latin America. He also holds Peruvian citizenship and spent roughly two decades serving as a missionary and bishop in Peru before taking on leadership roles at the Vatican.

POPE LEO XIV HIT IN THE FACE BY FLYING ROSARY DURING FAREWELL MASS IN PERU, VIDEO SHOWS

Pope Leo XIV appeared to be struck near the eye by a rosary Monday as he reached out to catch prayer beads tossed toward his popemobile ahead of a farewell Mass in Lima, Peru. (Pilar Olivares/Reuters)

It was while riding in the popemobile through huge crowds toward the Mass in Lima on Nov. 16 that Leo was struck near the eye by a rosary thrown from the crowd.

"The affection shown by the Peruvian people, including the person who, with such great faith, simply wanted to offer me a rosary, is something one carries in one's heart — or perhaps in one's eye," he joked about the incident.

"These are experiences that leave a lasting mark on one's life."

"They bear witness to genuine enthusiasm, deep faith, and the desire to receive the Lord's blessing," he added before describing the crowds' devotion.

"Some even tried to get past the National Police barricades. They simply wanted to live, feel, and experience this faith," he said.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title: What is Trump hoping to achieve at APEC meeting in China?
articles.excerpt: United States President Donald Trump will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, this week, where he is expected to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and h...
articles.body_text:
United States President Donald Trump will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, this week, where he is expected to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and hold a three-way meeting with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

A Trump-Xi meeting on the sidelines of the economic summit, which includes 21 Pacific Rim member economies, would be the third time the two superpower leaders have met this year.

The prior meetings – with Xi hosting Trump in Beijing in May and Trump hosting Xi at the White House in September – were heavy on ceremonial pomp, as both leaders sought to portray a sense of stability in the consequential relationship, but light on meaningful breakthroughs.

Experts predicted a similar approach in Shenzhen, as topics of AI regulation, trade and the self-ruling island of Taiwan will again loom large.

The summit comes just days after Democrats won commanding control of both chambers of the US Congress, a shift that will likely serve as a major check on the US president in his final two years in office. Beijing, meanwhile, is increasingly looking beyond the Trump era to see what comes next.

“Trump will work to strengthen his rapport with Xi, but the meeting is unlikely to produce any substantive breakthroughs,” Ali Wyne, a senior research and advocacy adviser on US-China relations at Crisis Group, said.

As for Russia, Putin’s foreign policy adviser Yury Ushakov told reporters on Monday that “the significance and symbolism” of the meetings between the three superpower leaders “are hard to overestimate”.

Neither side has yet released a formal agenda for an expected Trump-Xi meeting, although the White House announced plans for the two countries to support each other at APEC and at the G20 summit in Florida in December.

“The two countries agreed to build a constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness, and reciprocity,” according to a White House statement.

As in previous meetings, AI regulation is set to loom large. Both the US and China, as industry leaders, have faced pressure to jointly agree to safeguards on the transformative technology.

In September, both sides pledged to set up a mechanism to quickly communicate AI-related incidents and to hold a dialogue on emerging risks.

Still, the Trump administration has repeatedly downplayed the need to integrate developmental guardrails. Following the White House meeting, Trump said the US would “not be putting on brakes” on the AI industry.

Speaking at a National Committee on US-China Relations event last week, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said both sides “expect to exchange best practices for evaluating and testing advanced models before their release, and for keeping human judgment firmly in command of this technology”.

“As we do so, we should harbour no illusions about the differences between the United States and China,” he said. “And our approach to every challenge, likewise, will not always converge.”

The recent resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, which followed revelations that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, will also loom large over any Trump-Xi meeting, even if it is not directly addressed.

Huang’s close relationship with Trump, including accompanying the US president to Beijing during his May visit, and his ties to alleged spy Alice Huang have renewed questions about the influence he exerted over the US government as he pushed to ease restrictions on the sale of advanced AI chips to Beijing.

Trump administration Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has faced particular scrutiny, including from prominent members of the Republican Party, over his reportedly lax enforcement of export controls related to China.

“Trump will be under enormous pressure from Congress and members of his own administration to raise the scandal and warn Xi that their relationship could suffer if Trump concludes that Xi has been deploying Huang and other prominent business executives to sabotage US artificial intelligence efforts,” according to Crisis Group’s Wyne.

Still, some experts expect it to have little bearing on his interaction with his Chinese counterpart.

Gabriel Wildau, managing director at the advisory firm Teneo, told Al Jazeera last week that Trump “shows no sign that he intends to disrupt the current US-China rapprochement”.

The Reuters news agency reported on Friday that US officials said Trump is not expected to raise the issue of Alice Huang with Xi.

China has denied Alice Huang was working as a spy on its behalf.

Trump has already bucked longstanding US policy on Taiwan during his recent meeting with Xi.

Following the Beijing summit in May, Trump told reporters he had discussed US arms sales to the self-governing island, which Beijing claims as its own, “in great detail” with the Chinese president.

The US has provided arms to Taiwan since 1979 as mandated under the Taiwan Relations Act. But under the 1982 Six Assurances document, Washington has not consulted with China on such sales.

In a subsequent Fox News interview, Trump also referred to Taiwan as a “very good negotiating chip” with China. He has since held up approval of a $14bn arms package earmarked for the island.

The language “invites Beijing to expect something in return for each future approval”, Bonnie Glaser and Noah Munk of The German Marshall Fund of the United States (GMF) wrote in a recent analysis.

“The more successful that bargaining appears, the more Beijing will press it, and the more it will treat the next notification as a concession from Washington rather than a routine measure under the Taiwan Relations Act,” they wrote.

For its part, the White House has defended the delay, citing limited production capacity, particularly amid the US-Israel war with Iran, as well as the delicate nature of the US-China trade truce.

Democratic control of Congress, and general bipartisan support for Taiwan, could see pressure increase on the issue in Trump’s final two years in office.

“Today, the results of the midterm elections are on balance favourable for Taiwan,” Robert Sutter, a professor of international affairs at George Washington University, wrote recently for the ThinkChina publication.

Taiwan, a member of APEC, will be represented at the summit by Acer Group founder Stan Shih.

US-China trade relations took a nosedive at the start of Trump’s second term, with the US president initially launching 10 percent tariffs on China for allegedly failing to crack down on the trade of fentanyl precursors.

By April, additional US tariffs on Chinese goods had reached 145 percent, while China’s retaliatory tariffs on US goods reached 125 percent.

Agreements to bring down the temperature faltered until Trump and Xi agreed to a yearlong truce in Busan, South Korea, in October of last year. The deal was extended through January 10, 2027, following Xi’s White House visit in September.

A particular issue has been US access to China’s rare earth minerals, which was severely restricted. Still, a recent analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) found that US imports of China’s rare earth minerals during the first 11 months of the agreement remained 75 percent lower than prior to the escalation.

“The recurring challenge is the persistent gap between China’s diplomatic commitments and actual export volumes,” the analysts wrote. “Despite successive agreements in Switzerland, London, and South Korea intended to restore supplies, shipments of controlled rare earth materials to the United States remain approximately 75 percent below pre-restriction levels.”

US agricultural exports were also hard hit during the trade war, an issue for farmers that resonated during the midterm elections. In recent meetings, China has agreed to buy 25 million metric tonnes of US soya beans, as well as what the White House has described as $17bn per year in US agricultural products in 2026, 2027, and 2028.

Those purchases have also lagged behind the commitments.

The most significant outcome of this year’s APEC summit may be the three-way meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin.

Such a meeting would likely be seen as a massive boon for Putin.

“By sitting down with the leaders of the world’s two most powerful countries in a trilateral format, Putin will be recognised as a major player on the world stage rather than a pariah,” Ryan Hass, a China expert at the Brookings Institution, wrote in a recent analysis.

Xi, in turn, would “bask in the glow of China serving as the convener and agenda-setter for how China, Russia, and the United States will relate to each other”.

The benefit for Trump, who the White House says will focus on denuclearisation efforts, remains less clear, according to experts.

“A trilateral meeting would showcase the extent to which both Trump and Putin seek to curry favour with Xi,” Crisis Group’s Wyne said.

“It would also further unnerve US allies and partners that fear Trump’s openness to an informal ‘G2’ or ‘G3’ arrangement,” he said, referring to a global realignment that bypasses other world powers.

articles.title: Prosecutors allege man ‘destroyed’ US military plane at Irish airport
articles.excerpt:
An axe-wielding man breached a security perimeter and damaged a United States military C-130 aircraft at an Irish airport, prosecutors have alleged.

Daithi O’Corrain, 48, was indicted by a grand jury...
articles.body_text:
An axe-wielding man breached a security perimeter and damaged a United States military C-130 aircraft at an Irish airport, prosecutors have alleged.

Daithi O’Corrain, 48, was indicted by a grand jury in New York on Monday, with the indictment unsealed on Tuesday. Prosecutors claim that the Irish man left the plane “effectively destroyed”.

An online fundraiser organised by people describing themselves as O’Corrain’s friends and comrades said he disarmed the C-130 in protest at the US-Israel war on Iran and Washington’s support for Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza – a flashpoint in Ireland, where many people have expressed solidarity with Palestinians.

“An inspiring act of direct action was carried out at Shannon Airport to resist the unwanted presence of the US Military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war & support of Israel’s genocide,” organiser Tracey Ryan wrote.

O’Corrain is expected to be “brought to and arrested in the Southern District of New York”, the indictment said. He faces up to 10 years in prison if convicted of destruction of government property.

O’Corrain plotted the attack for months, US prosecutors said, searching online for information about the construction of the C-130, a quad-engine turboprop mainly used for transporting equipment and personnel.

According to prosecutors, he then breached security at Shannon Airport on April 11 and barricaded himself inside the parked aircraft.

He allegedly cut wires and hydraulic lines and smashed every gauge in the cockpit.

O’Corrain also inflicted damage on the exterior of the aircraft with an axe, prosecutors said, and poured ball bearings into the transport plane’s fuel tanks.

“As a result of O’Corrain’s attack, the aircraft was effectively destroyed,” the office of the US Attorney for the Southern District of New York said in a statement.

“The damage inflicted rendered the aircraft inoperable, and the aircraft – worth approximately $60 million – will not return to active flight status.”

Shannon Airport, which was used by US President Donald Trump and Air Force One during his visit to Ireland in September, has had several security breaches in the last 18 months, including three people who were accused of spray-painting a US military plane and three others who drove to a restricted area where a US military jet was parked.

articles.title: Man charged over ‘brutal attack’ on Somali-American in Minnesota
articles.excerpt:
A 25-year-old man has been charged in Minnesota with attempted murder and carjacking after an attack on a Somali-American Uber driver that prosecutors describe as “incredibly brutal”.

Mohamed Yusuf s...
articles.body_text:
A 25-year-old man has been charged in Minnesota with attempted murder and carjacking after an attack on a Somali-American Uber driver that prosecutors describe as “incredibly brutal”.

Mohamed Yusuf suffered broken ribs, a broken leg, spinal injuries, collapsed lungs and significant internal bleeding after being strangled with a seatbelt and run over by his own car in the city of Hopkins early on Saturday, according to court documents. His family said he was in a coma.

“It was an incredibly brutal attack,” Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said on Tuesday.

She said her office had charged Samit Apurva Patel with one count of second-degree attempted murder and one count of first-degree carjacking for the assault on Yusuf on November 14. Patel was taken into custody on Saturday.

Yusuf’s family claimed the attack was driven by hate, while civil rights advocates demanded a hate crime investigation.

Prosecutors said the evidence could not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Patel’s behaviour was motivated by bias, though that “does not diminish the pain that the family and the Somali community is feeling right now”, Moriarty said.

The court filing said Yusuf was on the phone with his brother, who is also an Uber driver, when Yusuf picked up the passenger just before 1am on Saturday. His brother allegedly heard the passenger tell Yusuf that he did not like the name Mohamed.

“He was apparently pulled out of the car and was standing there when Patel drove over him and might have circled back and driven over him again,” Moriarty said.

Patel’s parents called police for a wellness check after he arrived home appearing intoxicated and “exhibiting signs of emotional distress and belligerent behavior”, according to the court filing.

When the officers arrived, they found Yusuf’s car in the driveway with the exterior and driver’s seatbelt damaged. The phone call with Yusuf’s brother was still active through the car’s system, court records show.

Officers said Patel told them he had been drinking and “admitted he took an Uber home, but he claimed not to know where his Uber driver was”, the filing says.

Officers found Yusuf in a patch of burs in a ditch off the side of the road using location data from his smartwatch and a drone with thermal imaging.

Uber said in a statement that it was horrified by the attack, that it has been in touch with the driver’s family and has banned the rider from the platform.

Rights advocates have raised concerns about rhetoric against Somali Americans by US President Donald Trump and his allies, and condemned his immigration crackdown in Minnesota.

US rights advocates have also noted rising Islamophobia over the past two-plus decades following the September 11, 2001, attacks, and more recently due to anti-immigration policies, rising white supremacy movements and the fallout from Israel’s war on Gaza.

articles.title: White House withdraws nomination of Heidi Overton to lead FDA
articles.excerpt:
Move to drop Trump ally and prominent abortion opponent comes a day before key Senate health committee vote

The White House has dropped its nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Admin...
articles.body_text:
Move to drop Trump ally and prominent abortion opponent comes a day before key Senate health committee vote

The White House has dropped its nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration, a White House official told the Guardian.

Donald Trump nominated Overton – a physician and prominent abortion opponent – in August. Overton has spent most of her professional career working directly for Trump or conservative groups aligned with his agenda. Her nomination in August was seen as a move to bring a stabilizing Trump loyalist to the agency after a tumultous year under Trump’s first FDA commissioner, Marty Makary.

But Overton faced bipartisan questions in the Senate about her willingness to break from Trump, particularly on his unsupported claims about the dangers of childhood vaccines.

Republican senator Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana doctor who chairs the Senate health committee, said earlier on Tuesday that he remained undecided about her nomination ahead of a Senate health, labor and pensions committee vote scheduled for Wednesday.

Cassidy had previously called Overton’s support for Trump’s plan to break up combination vaccines – including the measles, mumps and rubella shot – “almost disqualifying”. And he pressed her during a September hearing about her scientific independence and willingness to push back against Trump and health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, a longtime vaccine critic.

A prominent reproductive rights group celebrated the White House’s decision to withdraw Overton’s nomination.

Mini Timmaraju, the president and CEO of Reproductive Freedom for All, formerly Naral Pro-Choice America, said: “Heidi Overton posed a serious threat to the future of medication abortion access. Voters rejected that anti-abortion agenda nationwide, and our members kept the pressure on to tank her confirmation. If Republicans try to rush through another nominee who threatens our healthcare, we’re ready to keep fighting.”

As the head of the FDA, Overton would have overseen the agency that regulates medication abortions. In a 2023 policy brief for the conservative America First Policy Institute, Overton said Congress should strictly regulate the abortion pill mifeprestone “to protect women and children”, criticized federal policies that allow for the mailing of abortion pills and wrote that abortion “is corrosive to children, women, and society broadly”.

To win confirmation, Overton would have needed the votes of all 12 Republicans on the Senate health, education, labor and pensions committee. Democrats hold 11 seats. Without support of the committee, Overton faced little chance of winning a full Senate vote on chamber floor.

Republicans are racing to try to confirm all of Trump’s current nominees before they hand over power to Senate Democrats in January.

articles.title: Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as firm reports bumper results
articles.excerpt:
Jensen Huang and Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress

Nvidia's quarterly sales doubled to top $100bn for the first time as the company insisted it has no plans to reinstate ousted co-founder Jensen Hu...
articles.body_text:
Jensen Huang and Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress

Nvidia's quarterly sales doubled to top $100bn for the first time as the company insisted it has no plans to reinstate ousted co-founder Jensen Huang.

In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit, interim chief executive Colette Kress said it is "business as usual" and told investors: "We've got this."

The company's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier, reaching $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading.

Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China.

"The board does not intend to reinstate him," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said during a call on Tuesday with financial analysts.

The company's profits also doubled from a year ago. For the quarter, which covered the three months to 25 October, profit hit $65bn. Its revenue from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn in the same period.

Going forward, the company said its rapid growth is poised to continue, and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter.

Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?

Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure that Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worries that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader.

"The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."

Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout that is happening throughout the technology industry.

"It is business as usual," she said. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."

She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects".

"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."

The interim CEO also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre semiconductors to China.

The Hopper technology is in Nvidia's advanced H200 processors, which the firm won approval to sell in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.

They had previously been restricted over concerns that selling them to China would give its industries and military an edge over the US.

Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments had been stopped.

The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal

Jensen Huang says he would be 'honoured' to return as Nvidia CEO if board asked him

Despite board chairman Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analysts' questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement.

He said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection.

"With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new CEO will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person."

Michael Monaghan from investment firm Founder ETFs is among those who want Huang back in the top job at Nvidia.

The Nvidia investor told the BBC that he is waiting to see the results of a thorough investigation into Huang's actions, instead of relying on "salacious allegations" made in the media.

Nvidia's strong earnings are "from the machine that Jensen built" and a company tends to lose "its shine and vision" after an iconic founder leaves, Monaghan said.
