articles.title: Trump defends commerce secretary Lutnick for allegedly slow-walking Nvidia chip export restrictions – live
articles.excerpt:
President backs Lutnick after treasury secretary Scott Bessent blamed commerce department for delays in blocking advance AI chip exports

Donald Trump also defended his commerce secretary Howard Lutni...
articles.body_text:
President backs Lutnick after treasury secretary Scott Bessent blamed commerce department for delays in blocking advance AI chip exports

Donald Trump also defended his commerce secretary Howard Lutnick today, after he came under fire for allegedly slow-walking export restrictions on Nvidia chips to China. This comes after the company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, was ousted from his role following a revelation that he had a close relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), allegedly a Chinese operation.

Lutnick is now set to testify before Congress about delays by the commerce department in adding Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is associated with Alice Huang and has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in recent years, to Washington’s blacklist of companies that the US considers a risk to national security despite reported concerns within the administration.

Today, Trump justified any delayed action by Lutnick. “If you didn’t delay it, if you did do something, you could have a blow up with China. We’re having a very good relationship with China right now,” Trump said.

Lutnick is currently traveling with the president and other senior officials and cabinet members to Manila.

Meanwhile, Scott Bessent, Trump’s treasury secretary, said that he has “for months” been in favor of putting Megaspeed on the blacklist – but Lutnick’s commerce department “has the pen”, in an interview with CNBC last week.

“You will have to ask them about their internal process,” he added on Friday.

As the leadership battle for Senate majority leader heats up between progressive Democrat Chris Van Hollen and Chuck Schumer, the current minority leader, we’re watching for more on how the two are securing support of the wider caucus.

While several Democrats have said they don’t intend to back Schumer, they haven’t necessarily pledged to support Van Hollen.

Democratic Senator-elect Josh Turek, who flipped Iowa’s open seat in the recent midterms, told reporters today that he’d spoken to both lawmakers but is still waiting for “further plans” from them about how they will deal with affordability in the US.

“I like both,” Turek added. “I have not given my allegiance to any leadership or any party, and I told Iowans I was going to sit down with them and say: ‘What are you going to do for Iowa?’”

As Donald Trump and tech leaders clamor for his return as Nvidia’s CEO, the company’s board of directors is reportedly not considering bringing back Jensen Huang.

The board is focused on an investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back, CNBC reports this morning, citing a person familiar with the matter. Reuters hears the same, also citing a person familiar.

Huang resigned on Thursday after reports that he had at least two extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate.

Elon Musk and other tech bosses have called for Huang’s reinstatement, amid reports the AI figurehead is already plotting a return to the chip company, just days after he was ousted. An open letter that has more than 165,000 signatories demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.

Here’s Trump expressing his support for the return of Huang and saying he “would not mind” him being reinstated.

The secluded island of Ni‘ihau has long been a Republican stronghold in deep blue Hawai‘i. Ni‘ihauans have an unusual tendency to unanimously support conservative candidates, like in 2020, when all 43 Ni‘ihauan voters cast their ballots for Donald Trump.

This has been the case since as far back as the early 1900s, when Ni‘ihau’s ballots were sometimes relayed to the neighboring island of Kaua‘i via carrier pigeon. The headline of one characteristic 1939 Honolulu Star Bulletin article reads – “Ni‘ihau Casts 59 Votes All For GOP as Usual.” Bush beat Kerry 39-0, Reagan beat Carter 56-1, and Nixon beat Kennedy 99-0.

But this month, for the first time in recent memory, the island backed a Democrat for governor, casting 14 of their 21 votes for governor Josh Green and lieutenant governor Derek Kawakami. Has Ni‘ihau been caught up in the blue tsunami?

Donald Trump’s efforts to blame Friday’s four-hour nationwide flight stoppage – and the resulting travel chaos – on Democrats are “absurd”, an incoming Democratic member of Congress said yesterday.

The president remained largely silent and out of public view as air travel shut down on Friday, but yesterday he emerged to issue a series of posts blaming the incident on the Biden administration, despite Trump being in office for the last two years in which time Republicans have had control of Congress. He has continued this blame game today (see our earlier post).

Dan Koh, a US House representative-elect from Massachusetts and former Biden administration official, blasted the effort to cast aside blame.

“It’s kind of revisionist history – you might as well start blaming Ronald Reagan for the FAA strike in the 80s as part of this, too,” he said yesterday during an appearance on MS NOW’s The Weekend. “It’s absurd.”

Koh said Joe Biden secured “historic funding not only to the FAA but over a trillion dollars of infrastructure money” between Trump’s two presidencies. But, Koh added, “a lot of it … Donald Trump has reversed on the grounds of it being too woke”, invoking a term that those on the political right use to refer to things they perceive to be overly leftist.

The congressman-elect said he talks frequently with mayors and city council members in his district about “all this money that would help them with upgrades to transportation including flights” – but “they don’t even know if they’re going to get any more because the [Trump] administration has not even gotten back to them on the status.” He added:

double quotation markThis is the reality: Donald Trump likes to say it’s Biden’s fault, but it’s actually his policies that are stopping the funding from hitting the towns and cities.

Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, announced on Monday that he was disbanding a controversial city police unit that has faced criticism over the years from civil rights groups who have accused the unit of using excessive force and unduly aggressive tactics against protesters.

In a video released on Monday morning, Mamdani said the move stemmed from a campaign pledge he made to disband the New York City police department’s strategic response group (SRG). “Today, we are keeping that promise,” Mamdani said in the video.

An accompanying joint statement from Mamdani and NYPD commissioner Jessica Tisch said the overhaul would “transform how the city prepares for and responds to protests, placing communication, de-escalation and civilian coordination at the center of our approach, while protecting New Yorkers’ constitutional right to protest”.

Along with eliminating the SRG, which was founded in 2015 ostensibly to focus on counter-terrorism, Mamdani and Tisch’s statement also said that the city planned to establish a “first-of-its-kind, civilian-led Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division (CDDD)” within the mayor’s office of community safety.

That division will not have weapons or arrest powers, unlike the SRG, according to the announcement.

The city will also establish what they described as a “specialized dialogue team” that will be known as the “First Amendment Support Team” (Fast) within the NYPD’s community affairs bureau, Mamdani and Tisch’s statement said. The creation of Fast is meant to “improve the NYPD’s protest response”, and it will consist of 30 uniformed officers trained in communication and de-escalation, the mayor and police commissioner said.

Donald Trump also defended his commerce secretary Howard Lutnick today, after he came under fire for allegedly slow-walking export restrictions on Nvidia chips to China. This comes after the company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, was ousted from his role following a revelation that he had a close relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), allegedly a Chinese operation.

Lutnick is now set to testify before Congress about delays by the commerce department in adding Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is associated with Alice Huang and has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in recent years, to Washington’s blacklist of companies that the US considers a risk to national security despite reported concerns within the administration.

Today, Trump justified any delayed action by Lutnick. “If you didn’t delay it, if you did do something, you could have a blow up with China. We’re having a very good relationship with China right now,” Trump said.

Lutnick is currently traveling with the president and other senior officials and cabinet members to Manila.

Meanwhile, Scott Bessent, Trump’s treasury secretary, said that he has “for months” been in favor of putting Megaspeed on the blacklist – but Lutnick’s commerce department “has the pen”, in an interview with CNBC last week.

“You will have to ask them about their internal process,” he added on Friday.

Trump also continued to shift responsibility to Joe Biden administration for the national ground stop over the weekend, that saw thousands of flights.

This is just the second nationwide ​ground stop of all departures since the 9/11 attacks. The previous one came in January 2023, when the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) paused all ⁠domestic departures for less than two hours.

“I hate to blame anybody, but the Biden administration hooked up a lot of copper into glass, and if you know anything about electrical engineering you cannot hook up copper into glass,” Trump claimed. “A lot of money was wasted, but the equipment is very old, in some cases more than 50 years old, and we essentially want to blow it up and put a new one in, and we can do it simultaneously with very little trouble. So that’s what we’re doing, but we need the funding to get it done. But essentially what you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack.”

Trump’s claims comes after Congress, under Republican control, passed a $12.5bn air traffic control package in 2025, as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The president, however, appeared convinced that lawmakers would be now more willing to allocate more funding to upgrade the systems. “I think the one good thing that comes out of it I’m sure Congress now will give us the money,” he told reporters today.

Over the weekend, Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, said in an interview with ABC News that the existing funding did not provide money for “a new architecture for telecom”.

“I don’t have any money given by Congress to build a new software system to manage the airspace. They’re very specific on how we spend the 12.5 and none of the money goes to this telecom that I have to build,” he said.

However, the top House Democrats on two key transportation and aviation committees said in a statement that, as of now, $8bn remains unobligated and $11bn is unspent.

Today, Trump also scolded a reporter for questioning why he has spent considerable time devoting energy and resources to White House renovation projects, instead of the FAA upgrades.

“You’re so pathetic,” he said. “I have a responsibility to make sure the symbol of our country is in decent shape, and it takes me 10 minutes a day. Very little time … That building, if you looked a year ago when I came back, was in horrible condition.”

Donald ⁠Trump said today that he ⁠would ​not ‌mind ‌seeing Jensen ‌Huang reinstated as the chief executive ‌officer of ​Nvidia.

Trump is speaking to reporters now, ahead of his trip to Manila to attend the Asean summit.

The president added that the suggestion that Huang could return to Nvidia is not a bad idea. He says the ex-CEO has learned a lesson, and denies that national security has been put at risk.

“I think having Jensen go back – a lot of people are asking Jensen - they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea,” the president said.

That’s quite an intervention, as an open letter circulates calling for the chip giant to reinstate Huang.

Elon Musk and a host of other tech bosses have called for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia, amid reports the former chief executive is already plotting a return to the chip company just four days after his resignation.

An open letter that has more than 165,000 signatories demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.

Huang’s resignation on Thursday ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI company he co-founded, after reports he had at least two extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate.

According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed a possible return to the company with people close to him. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together ⁠a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby ​for the former Nvidia ‌CEO’s return ‌and would try to garner support from ‌the White House.

“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the person said, adding that the efforts had Huang’s support.

One quick note on the US Senate race in Alaska. According to the state’s election laws, if no candidate manages to cross the 50% threshold, that triggers a ranked-choice runoff where the candidate with fewest votes is eliminated but their vote goes to their second choice (which they mark on their ballot). This happens in rounds until the candidate with the most votes wins.

Donald Trump will begin his day in Washington, before traveling to Manila, Philippines, for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit.

Trump’s first order or business will be his first meeting with the “Quad” alliance since he returned to the White House last year. This group includes Indian prime minister Narendra Modi, Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese, and Sanae Takaichi, the Japanese prime minister.

Then, later this week, Trump will take part in the first trilateral summit between China’s Xi Jinping and Russian president Vladimir Putin.

Here’s more about what we can expect this week from my colleague Robert Tait:

Democrat Mary Peltola is leading Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in the nail-biting race for US Senate in Alaska.

With 97% of the ballots counted, Peltola – a former congresswoman – has 49.9% of the vote and only needs more than 50% to win.

At present, Sullivan only has 46% of the vote. This would be the Democrats’ ninth flip of the midterms cycle and the first time the party has won a US Senate since 2009.

On Sunday Trump continued to blast Ana Reyes, the federal judge appointed by Joe Biden, who has temporarily blocked construction on the historic Washington public golf course that the president wants to turn it ⁠into a championship-level course.

“Why would a judge want to delay taking a terrible and very unsafe golf course, one that is mocked all over D.C.(and far beyond!), instead of quickly turning it into a great and admired one?” Trump wrote on Truth Social, noting that his administration plans to appeal the ruling. “Time is of the essence, or golf seasons, jobs, prestige, and much money, will be lost!”

US air travel was slowly returning to normal on Monday after three days of widespread disruption following an extraordinary no-takeoff order issued by US aviation authorities.

The ground stop issued on Friday afternoon was only the second time such a directive had been issued nationwide in the busy US airspace since planes were grounded following the 9/11 attacks and was blamed by the Trump administration on a faulty upgrade to communications equipment.

On Monday morning, more than 250 US-related flights – those traveling within, into or out of the United States – scheduled for the same day were cancelled, according to industry tracker FlightAware.

That marked a dramatic shift from the more than 2,300 flights cancelled on Sunday.

There were delays to more than 700 US-related flights scheduled for Monday, compared to more than 10,000 the previous day, AFP reported.

A progressive and onetime presidential candidate, Senator Elizabeth Warren is a vocal Wall Street critic and has repeatedly condemned the Trump administration and its policies.

She is the top Democrat on the Senate banking committee, and is widely expected to become chair when Democrats ⁠take over Congress, Reuters reported.

The US Department of ⁠Justice on Sunday warned her of potential “significant legal consequences” if she fails ⁠to preserve records related to ⁠investigations into Donald Trump.

Aaron Reitz’s letter to Warren cited her statements on investigating corporate leaders. “The ​context sends a strong ​smoke signal: you intend to target private ​individuals close to president Trump,” he wrote.

Other Democratic lawmakers who have ​received similar letters include ‌Senators Richard Blumenthal ​and Elissa Slotkin ​as well as Representative Robert Garcia, who is in line to lead the House oversight committee.

Political experts and Trump’s opponents have raised concerns about efforts by the Republican president and his administration to target their own critics and political opponents.

Donald Trump is embarking on his first overseas trip since his Republican party’s thumping midterm repudiation by US voters, in what may herald a renewed focus on foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency.

The US president will meet his Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, for their first trilateral summit, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Before that, he will land in Manila in the Philippines on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit.

At the Asean summit, Trump is expected to sign a trade agreement with Thailand, push deals with other countries and lobby fellow leaders to favour the US over China on artificial intelligence.

He will also take part in the first leaders’ meeting of the Quad partnership – consisting of the US, Japan, India and Australia – since he returned to the White House in January 2025.

White House officials said the president would be accompanied to Apec by Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX entrepreneur who spent almost $500m (£380m) unsuccessfully supporting Republican candidates in this month’s midterms. The reason for Musk’s presence has not been explained.

The China leg of the trip will take place amid the continuing fallout from the Nvidia spying scandal, which prompted the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, to resign amid revelations he had had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Trump is under pressure to raise the matter with Xi when they hold a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of Apec.

The US president has said he does not plan to bring up the subject; administration officials insist he will not do so and that the meeting will be dedicated to implementing a trade agreement between the two superpowers.

Democratic US senator Chris Van Hollen on Sunday escalated his bid to lead his party’s incoming Senate majority rather than Chuck Schumer, asserting that he has a path to victory amid a dedicated campaign that includes a series of television appearances.

Van Hollen, a Maryland progressive, appeared on Sunday on CNN, ABC and Fox News as he continues to make his case for why his peers in the Senate should reject Schumer, who has led the Democratic caucus for nearly a decade.

On CNN’s State of the Union, he reaffirmed that he believes he has a path to victory, citing support and a widespread openness to change within the Senate Democratic caucus.

“This really is a response to the call of the voters, who clearly rejected Donald Trump and his awful policies, but they haven’t fully hired the Democrats,” Van Hollen said, alluding to how the US president’s Republican party lost control of Congress during the 3 November midterm elections.

“They’ve given us a chance, and I think we need to earn their trust. And I think that begins by not going back to business as usual.”

Van Hollen criticized reports that Schumer’s team may move the Senate caucus leadership election date earlier than 1 December. He contended that the caucus should have a debate about the group’s direction as the Democrats assume control of Congress in January for the second half of Trump’s second presidency.

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, the likely incoming chair of the Senate banking committee, was warned by the US Department of ⁠Justice of potential “significant legal consequences” if she fails ⁠to preserve records related to ⁠investigations into ​president Donald Trump.

It is the latest warning sent by the justice department to congressional Democrats about their potential plans to investigate the ⁠administration or Trump associates, Reuters reported.

Trump last week ordered the department to look into Democratic lawmakers for “threatening” people, and US attorney-general Todd Blanche subsequently indicated that ⁠his agency was prepared to battle congressional Democrats.

In a letter to Warren, US attorney Aaron ​Reitz in Houston told the Massachusetts Democrat ‌she appeared “eager to wield your ‌future gavel like a tomahawk, hunting for the scalps of president Trump’s private associates”.

Reitz told ‌her to preserve materials “relevant to your intent to weaponize congressional investigations and deprive citizens of their core constitutional rights”.

Notices to preserve records can presage investigations. Warren’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Reitz shared the letter on social media and Trump reposted it to his Truth Social account several hours later.

Warren and other Democrats have signaled ‌that when their party takes control of Congress in January, they plan to investigate large corporations, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and Elon ​Musk, the world’s richest person, among others.

Donald Trump is preparing to depart for Asia on Monday, turning his focus to economic deals and historic three-way nuclear talks with Russia and China as his administration adjusts to a new political reality in Washington. Trump’s departure comes after the often-omnipresent president had remained largely out of public sight for the past several days.

Van Hollen, a Maryland progressive, appeared on Sunday on CNN, ABC and Fox News as he continues to make his case for why his peers in the Senate should reject Schumer, who has led the Democratic caucus for nearly a decade.

US air travel disruptions continued for a third day with more than 10,000 flights affected on Sunday, but transportation secretary Sean Duffy predicted a return to normal by Monday even as airlines scrambled to get back on schedule following a systemwide ground stop.

After recently becoming the first Mississippi Democrat elected to the US Senate in more than four decades, Scott Colom pledged to try to ensure Trump “follows through on the commitments” he made while successfully running for a second presidency in 2024. Colom, while being interviewed by CNN host Dana Bash on Sunday, alluded to various campaign promises made by Trump – including lowering consumer prices, halting the seemingly endless wars waged under other presidential administrations, and fully releasing files related to the prosecution of Jeffrey Epstein, the late accused sex trafficker whose social circle encompassed the US and global elite.

articles.title: Dan Dakich rips into Lane Kiffin after LSU's loss to Texas eliminates Tigers from CFB Playoff picture
articles.excerpt: After blowing a fourth-quarter lead at home and falling 22-21 to Texas and Arch Manning, Lane Kiffin’s 6-4 Tigers are officially out of the College Football Playoff picture and Kiffin immediately went...
articles.body_text:
After blowing a fourth-quarter lead at home and falling 22-21 to Texas and Arch Manning, Lane Kiffin’s 6-4 Tigers are officially out of the College Football Playoff picture and Kiffin immediately went into excuse mode.

Lane Kiffin left Ole Miss a season ago in unprecedented fashion to take over an LSU program that he's described as "just different." Part of what makes coaching the Tigers different is the expectations, and Kiffin has failed to meet a single one in his first season in Baton Rouge.

During Monday's edition of 'Don't @ Me with Dan Dakich,' the OutKick host agreed with Kiffin's assessment that LSU is 'just different,' but not in a positive way.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

"Kiffin told us all that LSU is different," Dakich explained. "I know it's different; it's the best college football program in the country they tell us when it goes to history, tradition, money, fan support, facility. That's what they tell me. Different.

"Different how now? It's got four losses. That's different for an elite school. Not sure very many elite football programs have four losses: first year of a coach, second year of a coach, or 20th year as a coach."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

While some may claim that Kiffin needs time to build something potentially special in Baton Rouge, that is an idea very tough to sell to an LSU fanbase living in the NIL era with a roster worth approximately $50 million.

Head coach Lane Kiffin of the LSU Tigers is in action against the Texas Longhorns at Tiger Stadium in Baton Rouge, La., on Nov. 14, 2026. (University Images via Getty Imag)

Speaking after his team's 22-21 loss at home to Texas on Saturday, a loss that ended all of LSU's hope of sneaking into the College Football Playoff, Kiffin made an interesting remark about his roster.

"We’ll have better rosters, and that’s no poor reflection upon these players," Kiffin said. "We just will. We will have been here. We’ll have built depth. We will. We won’t have senior days with two scholarship players."

LSU head coach Lane Kiffin works during fall practice at Tiger Stadium on Aug. 22, 2026, in Baton Rouge, La. (University Images via Getty Images)

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Dakich isn't out on the idea that Kiffin is just the perfect representation of what may just be the new school coach in modern-day college football.

"Maybe Kiffin represents the new school coach. Get in there, bulls— him, and then blame the players. And maybe that's the way it should be," Dakich said. "But when Kiffin blames the players, it's a lot different from a Nick Saban or Bob Knight blaming the players. It just is. It seems like excuse-making."

LSU's 6-4 record speaks for itself, but with two of the four losses coming at home in consecutive weeks, it makes the situation a bit more damning. If the Tigers don't manage to pull off an upset against Tennessee in Knoxville in their penultimate regular-season game, Kiffin could close out year one in Baton Rouge with his best win being a road victory at Auburn, a team that will likely finish the season at 7-5.

Kiffin's former team, Ole Miss, is also 6-4 on the year, but the Rebels own all bragging rights, having beaten the Tigers 32-24 earlier in the season.

Mark Harris is a writer for OutKick. Follow him on X @itismarkharris.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed’s victory is a blow to the politics of Islamophobia
articles.excerpt:
Professor Emerita of Media Studies at Fordham University, and former Director of Graduate Studies and the Peace and Justice Studies programme.

The blue wave that swept Republicans from their congress...
articles.body_text:
Professor Emerita of Media Studies at Fordham University, and former Director of Graduate Studies and the Peace and Justice Studies programme.

The blue wave that swept Republicans from their congressional majorities and brought Democrats back into the spotlight was called everything from a flood to a political earthquake. In a montage on The Daily Show, TV anchors reduced the night to a gleeful succession of words and phrases like “rout” and “shellacking”. On Zeteo’s election-night coverage with Mehdi Hasan, Prem Thakker coined the term “Tsunamanani”, a brief injection of comic irony amid serious news and analysis. The night was all those things.

Arguably the most significant victory of the congressional sweep was Abdul El-Sayed’s win over Trump-backed extremist Mike Rogers, whose candidacy was propped up by roughly $169 million in outside spending benefiting him, including spending by Republican super PACs tied to Donald Trump and Elon Musk. El-Sayed will be the first Muslim ever to grace the floor of the US Senate.

It was hard to look away from the joy on El-Sayed’s face as he shared the win. His words were just as striking, offering a vision of how American politics could be redirected towards peace and humanity. He told the crowd:“Michiganders, we want our taxes spent here, for schools here and healthcare here, and infrastructure here. We don’t want our money sent to do apartheid or genocide or war.”

When he said, “My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, and I am so proud and honored to stand here as your senator elect,” the crowd roared. Throughout the campaign, right-wing enthusiasts had used his whole name to brand him a “terrorist”, a “jihadist” and “a danger to the American public”. By pronouncing that name, complete with its Arabic intonation, he reclaimed what pundits and politicians, including Donald Trump, had spent months mocking. Later in the speech, El-Sayed joked, “Donald, look, I know you struggled with my name, so after JD swears me in in January, you could just go on and call me Senator.” The crowd roared again.

He also said, “You might have noticed, I always say Inshallah, or God willing, whenever the outcome of this race was mentioned. But today, tonight, we can turn that Inshallah into a…”

One minute and twenty seconds into his speech, the crowd shouted the answer together: “Alhamdulillah!” Then the hall filled with chants of “Abdul! Abdul! Abdul! Abdul! Abdul! Abdul! Abdul! Abdul!”

Still smiling, El-Sayed added, “For the right-wing ops, that just means praise be to God.”

When we heard the thunderous applause for his name and for “Alhamdulillah”, one of the most common yet sacred expressions in Islam, it felt as though a deeply entrenched stereotype about Islam and Muslims was being shattered, undermining the Islamophobia that has been used to stir fear and hatred in American politics.

With no meaningful policy accomplishments to point to and a wildly unpopular Donald Trump, Republicans resorted to a relentlessly bigoted smear campaign against El-Sayed.

The attacks he faced were part of a broader pattern of organised anti-Muslim prejudice, extending beyond bots and social media influencers into Republican politics and policymaking. As documented by the Center for the Study of Organized Hate, this hostility was being promoted through social media, legislation and a congressional caucus. According to the CSOH, 89 Republican elected officials took part in a coordinated anti-Muslim campaign over thirteen months: 46 of them published 1,111 social media posts, eight Sharia-related bills were introduced, and the Sharia-Free America Caucus grew to 62 members by April 2026.

Political advisers told El-Sayed that “someone with a name and my story, a Muslim, was unelectable”, as if anti-Muslim prejudice were an immovable grassroots bias. In reality, it was a prejudice deliberately cultivated and promoted with millions of dollars from billionaire funders, most of them Zionists.

When he entered the race for the US Senate, El-Sayed accepted the challenge of confronting the toxic Islamophobia built on the othering of Muslims and Islam. He refused to be demonised or to accept the artificial divide between “us” and “them”, responding with skilful verbal panache, always in his own words. At his final campaign rally, his wife, Dr Sarah Jukaku, introduced him with the words, “With Abdul, what you see is what you get … No corporation, no billionaire, no special interest. No one tells him what to do or what to say.” He offered voters an alternative, one notably humanistic and built on the promise of diversity, unity and a community of care. He put Gaza on the ballot as part of his vision.

Abdul El-Sayed is an American, a Midwesterner, a doctor and a husband who talks to his mother on a swing and pops up behind his grandparents on a video tape as a way to affirm his midwestern values. He worked in public health to help provide glasses to 16,000 children from low-income families in Detroit and Wayne County.

He is also a Muslim man with a long Middle Eastern name who speaks Arabic. As an American and a Muslim, he lays bare the lies that have dehumanised Muslims for so long. He visits farmers and residents across Michigan, including rural conservatives in the Upper Peninsula. When media pundits present his religion as a threat to Americans, he doesn’t back down. He talks openly about Islam and his identity, rejecting the narrow mindset of those who would brand him “foreign”. He places his religion in the context of Judaism and Christianity. In one video filmed at a Rosh Hashanah dinner, he talks with his Jewish hostesses, who recite a prayer before they share home-cooked kugel.

He invented new ways to talk about religion. In one campaign ad, he looks into the camera and says he prays, and that we all “need faith and hope that we can fix things”. The ad ends with, “I’m Abdul El-Sayed, a man of faith. That’s a good thing.”

In his speech on election night, he returned to the connection between war and the economy, which helps explain the blowback that cost Republicans control of Congress. He said, “It just shouldn’t be this hard to buy a second bag of groceries or fill your tank. It shouldn’t be this hard to see a doctor in the richest, most powerful country in the world. It shouldn’t be this hard to pay your taxes and know that that money’s going to be spent on you and your kids instead of dropping bombs on somebody else and their kids.” His words bring together the suffering of those caught in wars funded by our tax dollars and those deprived of their basic needs at home.

He used his voice to broaden the horizons of American politics, offering a vision that could reshape how we imagine America: a more expansive country where we all fit, embracing its diversity and rejecting the violence, hate and exclusion of the shrinking Trumpian world. He closed his speech with the call, “We deserve an America for all her kids. So Michigan, let’s go build it.”

Abdul El-Sayed’s accomplishment was a major blow to a world built on Arab and Muslim hate. He embodies, by contrast, a politics of joy, care, concern, justice and equality, and the possibility of an America so often lost to our imaginations in a world at war.

Now the so-called “centrist” or “moderate” Democrats must decide whether to champion a new anti-Islamophobic politics or keep taking money from hate mongers and mass murderers, and face the consequences of the same political blowback that cost Republicans their majorities.

A version of this article first appeared on Al Jazeera Arabic.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Trump backs calls for reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO
articles.excerpt:
As tech industry pushes for return, US president says he thinks Huang ‘learned a big lesson’

Donald Trump has expressed support for the return of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia, joinin...
articles.body_text:
As tech industry pushes for return, US president says he thinks Huang ‘learned a big lesson’

Donald Trump has expressed support for the return of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia, joining Silicon Valley heavyweights in backing the reinstatement of the AI figurehead.

The US president referred to a tech industry campaign for Huang’s rehabilitation, saying a “big group” of people would like him back.

“I think he learned a big lesson. I guess maybe one lesson is more important than ⁠another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that,” Trump told ​reporters as he left the ‌White House on ‌a trip to Asia. “He could return. There’s a big group of ‌people that would like him to return.”

The comments came as the US government announced a crackdown on companies such as Nvidia selling AI chips and servers to overseas datacentres that in turn are supplying computing power to China and other US adversaries.

Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and SpaceX, and a host of other tech bosses have signed an open letter calling for the reinstatement of Huang. The former Nvidia CEO resigned last Thursday amid reports of extramarital liaisons, including with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who is no relation. Days before, Huang had admitted being unfaithful to his wife without specifying who was involved.

Trump said on Monday: “Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy.” Trump has faced questions after it was reported that a US intelligence report about Huang’s relationship with the alleged spy was circulated among senior figures in his administration.

The reinstatement letter has more than 165,000 signatories and demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.

Huang’s resignation ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI company he co-founded.

According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed with people close to him a possible return to the company. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together ⁠a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby ​for his return ‌and would try to garner support from ‌the White House. The FT also reported on Monday that Nvidia’s board was not considering reinstating Huang.

One analyst downplayed the prospect of a Huang return, describing the notion of the ex-CEO’s reinstatement as “ridiculous”. Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the range of issues facing Huang and Nvidia, from personal conduct to questions over China, made an external candidate or the permanent appointment of the interim CEO – Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer – the best option.

“We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO, and for the company the best path forward is with a new external CEO or Colette,” he said, describing the petition as “noise and distraction”.

The new rule announced by the US government on Monday requires companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on ⁠them being illegally diverted.

“The rule ‌is designed to ​ensure that ​existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving datacentres in third countries,” the US Department of Commerce said.

Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy, worked as an executive at the Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. According to reports, Megaspeed is under suspicion of diverting powerful Nvidia chips to China in contravention of US export laws.

Megaspeed said on Sunday it was a “legitimate and lawful business” and that Huang had left the business in late 2025. It added that it complied “with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate”.

Nvidia shares opened down 2.7% on Monday, knocking about $100bn (£75.8bn) off Nvidia’s market capitalisation, lowering it to $3.82tn compared with $4.5tn before the scandal broke.

articles.title: Woman accusing David Walliams of grooming her backs staggered age of consent call
articles.excerpt:
Comments come after Mia Latter, who alleged she was raped by Russell Brand, had said she wanted a change in law

A woman who has accused David Walliams of grooming her has said she supports a staggere...
articles.body_text:
Comments come after Mia Latter, who alleged she was raped by Russell Brand, had said she wanted a change in law

A woman who has accused David Walliams of grooming her has said she supports a staggered age of consent.

Walliams, 55, has been accused of using his power and celebrity status to prey on young women and teenagers for sex, a joint investigation by the Guardian and ITV News has found.

Alex has alleged she was 15 and studying for her GCSEs when she first met Walliams, one of Britain’s best-known television personalities and top-selling children’s authors. She has alleged they began having sex when she was 17 and Walliams was 34.

Alex said she would have saved herself “a lot of trauma” if a staggered age of consent had been in place when she was a teenager.

“As a parent myself now, I would absolutely love for there to be a change of law. It’s something that is incredibly close to my heart, and I would feel very, very proud and happy if this could get over the line,” she told the Guardian and ITV News.

“It would protect everyone … from people that can abuse the law as it currently stands. I think it’s really important that teenagers are able to have relationships with each other. I think that the staggered element to it, I think works really well.”

Alex was speaking out after a woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 waived her right to anonymity to campaign for a staggered age of consent. Mia Latter told the Sunday Times she was in an abusive three-month relationship with Brand when he was 30 and she was 16.

She has called on the UK government to introduce a law that would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds.

Last week, Alex told the Guardian and ITV News that she was “groomed” by Walliams. “I never said no … but I felt unable to say anything or have any control in that situation once I was with him,” she said.

“OK, it’s legal to have sex when you’re 17, 18, 16 even, but the context of who you’re having sex with – if that person is double your age, if that person has known you from a young age and promised you things and is in a much bigger position of power than you, both in age, in work, in finance, in stature and size, like, everything, I really don’t think that’s OK.”

On Monday, Alex backed calls for a change in the law to “make it a lot harder for predators to act”.

She said she would have had a different perspective on Walliams’ behaviour had the law already been in place when she was a teenager.

“I grew up in a culture where it was normalised,” she said. “There were people saying to me at the time that this feels really wrong, but it was a bit more accepted, and it still happened more. And I think if I grew up in a world where [I] knew that that was illegal, and it was more clear that that shouldn’t have been happening, and that was wrong, then I think that I would have been a lot more wary of that and scared by it, and probably seen it more clearly for what it was at a younger age.

“I feel like if we can make the children of today know and understand from a young age that’s illegal, that’s against the law, that that person shouldn’t be talking to you in that way, shouldn’t be engaging with you in that way, and certainly shouldn’t be acting on it, it would make you pause and hope and I think it would definitely stop a lot of incidents happening.”

Walliams’ lawyers have said the suggestion he groomed Alex is false and that she did not raise, and he did not believe, that she had any concerns about the sex at the time. The lawyers add that Walliams was mortified to learn that their brief, consensual relationship had caused her sadness. Walliams has denied all the allegations against him.

Support for anyone affected by sexual abuse issues is available in the UK from Rape Crisis on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. Other international helplines are available for people affected by sexual abuse, childhood abuse, and people in crisis.

The ITV News documentary David Walliams: Power and Silence is available to watch on YouTube and ITVX.

articles.title: Customer's restaurant receipt sparks controversy after $6 charge appears for to-go box
articles.excerpt: A Charlotte, North Carolina, restaurant is responding to criticism after a customer questioned a $6 to-go box charge on her bill, saying the amount reflected a pricing adjustment rather than a fee for...
articles.body_text:
A Charlotte, North Carolina, restaurant is responding to criticism after a customer questioned a $6 to-go box charge on her bill, saying the amount reflected a pricing adjustment rather than a fee for a takeout container.

A North Carolina restaurant is responding to controversy after a customer shared a receipt on social media that appeared to show a $6 charge for a to-go box.

STATS, a restaurant and bar in Charlotte, claims the charge was not for a takeout container but was instead a price adjustment tied to its weekly pasta promotion.

The restaurant offers half-price pasta on Wednesdays, but the deal is available exclusively to customers dining inside the establishment.

RESTAURANT CHAIN MAY RETHINK CONTROVERSIAL 20% SERVICE CHARGE IN SOME VENUES AFTER CUSTOMER PUSHBACK

"However, if guests order dine-in promotional items for carry-out, the meal is adjusted to its regular price," STATS said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital. "In this case, the additional $6 was not a charge for a to-go container, but a computer adjustment to that original price."

The receipt shared on social media shows a $28 charge for Cajun Alfredo, as well as a $6 charge for the to-go box and a 3% service fee in the amount of $1.02.

A Charlotte, North Carolina, restaurant responded to a controversial charge on a customer's receipt after it showed a $6 fee for a to-go box on top of the $28 Cajun Alfredo (not pictured) special. (iStock)

A representative for STATS also provided additional details about the customer's order, saying the pasta included several extras.

"The customer also added two proteins (shrimp and fried salmon) and an additional vegetable (broccoli) to the pasta, which contributed to the overall cost of the dish," the representative told Fox News Digital. "The $6 adjustment was for requesting a dine-in special as carryout."

WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS ARE CHANGING DINING AS CUSTOMERS EAT HALF THEIR MEALS, TAKE REST HOME, CELEBRITY CHEF SAYS

But the customer clarified on social media that she frequents STATS and didn't go there "with the intention of getting a to-go meal at a cheaper price."

"I did not finish my pasta," she wrote. "Because I didn't finish my pasta, I got charged for a box or regular price, however you want to look at it. God forbid a girl gets full."

STATS says the charge wasn't for the box and that the meal was adjusted to its regular price since the deal only applies to those who dine at the establishment. But the customer claims she got full and asked to take the rest home. (iStock)

Fox News Digital reached out to the customer for comment.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"We understand the importance of clear communication, and we will adjust our systems to ensure itemized receipts more accurately reflect any price adjustments."

STATS acknowledged that its receipts may have contributed to confusion surrounding the charge and said changes are coming.

"We understand the importance of clear communication, and we will adjust our systems to ensure itemized receipts more accurately reflect any price adjustments," the statement said. "We also commit to clearly explaining our gratuity and promotional guidelines to guests."

STATS has been serving the Charlotte community for nearly a decade. (iStock)

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

STATS, which says it has served the Charlotte community for more than nine years, thanked customers for their continued support.

The restaurant did not specify when the receipt changes would take effect.

Peter Burke is a lifestyle editor with Fox News Digital. He covers various lifestyle topics, with an emphasis on food and drink.

articles.title: Why is China resisting a nuclear treaty with the US and Russia?
articles.excerpt:
The world’s top nuclear-armed countries are slated to hold their first-ever trilateral meeting soon as United States President Donald Trump pushes for a new nuclear arms treaty among them.

Trump will...
articles.body_text:
The world’s top nuclear-armed countries are slated to hold their first-ever trilateral meeting soon as United States President Donald Trump pushes for a new nuclear arms treaty among them.

Trump will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week in China’s Shenzhen, the White House confirmed.

Top of the agenda for Washington and Moscow is the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), which lapsed in February, marking the end of more than half a century of limits on US and Russian strategic nuclear weapons.

Trump previously rejected Russia’s proposal to extend the treaty, demanding instead a “new, improved and modernised” deal that includes Beijing.

But China has long signalled that it is not ready to join any nuclear arms control treaty.

New START was a treaty signed in 2010 by then-US President Barack Obama and Dmitry Medvedev, a close ally of Vladimir Putin who served as Russia’s president from 2008 to 2012. It was extended in 2021 for an additional five years when Joe Biden was the US president.

Under the agreement, Russia and the US were permitted to deploy no more than 1,550 strategic nuclear warheads and a maximum of 700 long-range missiles and bombers, had to impose a limit of 800 intercontinental ballistic missiles in deployment and grant permission for up to 18 inspections of strategic nuclear weapons sites annually by the other party.

New START collapsed in February after the five-year extension lapsed. This key accord was in turn built from earlier arms control treaties signed between Washington and Moscow.

The first of those, START I, was signed in 1991 between the US and the Soviet Union in the dying days of the Cold War. It remained in place until 2009 with the aim of capping US and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals.

START II, its successor, aimed to further reduce the number of deployed strategic nuclear warheads in addition to removing multiwarhead intercontinental ballistic missiles altogether. It was signed in 1993 but never came into force. Russia formally withdrew from it in 2002.

The Strategic Offensive Reductions Treaty (SORT) from 2003 to 2011, meanwhile, had the same purpose as START I but included less monitoring.

The COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 ended on-site inspections between the two nations in recent years, leaving them dependent on their own intelligence to judge compliance by the other side.

Still, the treaty offered some checks and balances to the two biggest nuclear powers in the world. Together, they possess about 86 percent of all nuclear warheads.

Trump has long wanted China included in the treaty because Washington believes an arms treaty involving only it and Moscow would no longer reflect the global nuclear balance of power.

“Today, the United States faces threats from multiple nuclear powers. In short, a bilateral treaty with only one nuclear power is simply inappropriate in 2026 and going forward,” US Undersecretary of State for Arms Control Thomas DiNanno said in February.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that same month said Trump made it clear that “to have true arms control in the 21st century, it’s impossible to do something that doesn’t include China because of their vast and rapidly growing stockpile”.

Washington also wants a successor treaty to address weapons not covered by New START.

DiNanno has said a new agreement would have to “account [for] all Russian nuclear weapons, both novel and existing strategic systems and [address] the breakout growth of Chinese nuclear weapons stockpiles”.

Beijing’s unwillingness is largely due to the sheer disparity of warheads it currently possesses when compared with the US and Russia.

It has an estimated 620 of them, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), well below the 800 cap each for Russia and the US under New START. Moscow and Washington now have more than 5,000 each, according to SIPRI data. While the US has retired a third of its nuclear warheads so far, Russia has retired less than a fourth.

China’s nuclear arsenal, however, is growing faster than any country’s – by about 100 new warheads a year since 2023, according to SIPRI.

In February, when New Start expired, Chinese officials explained their opposition to joining a nuclear weapons capping agreement.

“China’s nuclear forces are not on the same level as those of the United States and Russia, and China will not participate in disarmament negotiations at this stage,” Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Lin Jian said in a statement at the time.

This “structural asymmetry” explains China’s reluctance to join a nuclear arms control treaty with the US and Russia alongside its own domestic restraints, said Zhao Minghao, a professor at the Institute of International Studies at China’s Fudan University.

“China maintains a declared no-first-use policy and a ‘minimum deterrence’ posture – nuclear weapons as political instruments for assured retaliation, not warfighting,” Zhao told Al Jazeera.

“From Beijing’s perspective, its arsenal is already restrained by doctrine. The potential US-Russia-China treaty would cap its insurance while imposing intrusive verification on a comparatively small force.”

He also pointed to a “credibility problem”, given the US withdrawal from a number of related treaties, such as the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty and the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, which similarly seek to control missile numbers.

In China’s view, Washington has used arms control as a geopolitical instrument, Zhao said.

“Beijing’s strategic logic is that nuclear inferiority invites coercion – conventional or nuclear – while survivable second-strike capability neutralises it,” he said.

China’s smaller arsenal plays a role in its reluctance to join a nuclear arms treaty, but so does its ability to match US capabilities, said Sun Chenghao, a fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing.

“Chinese assessments also consider US missile defences, precision-strike capabilities and emerging technologies that could weaken its retaliatory capability,” Sun told Al Jazeera.

“An agreement limiting China’s forces while leaving those concerns untouched would have limited appeal.”

According to William Yang, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst for Northeast Asia, there’s no clear advantage for Beijing and any treaty would be viewed “as a mechanism designed to limit its nuclear modernisation”.

“As a result, Beijing prefers to maintain strategic autonomy in expanding its nuclear arsenal and modernising relevant defence capabilities,” Yang told Al Jazeera.

At the same time, China’s rapid nuclear expansion raises “legitimate questions about where Beijing intends to stop”, said Alejandro Reyes, an Asia Pacific policy specialist and professor at the University of Hong Kong,

“It is difficult to assess China’s ultimate ambitions when it provides little transparency about its nuclear programme. We should not assume that China seeks parity, but neither should we assume that its declared commitment to minimum deterrence fully explains its current build-up,” Reyes told Al Jazeera.

According to the analysts, China would engage in a trilateral framework only when the US and Russia first reduce their arsenals towards “genuine” parity.

Zhao argued that such a path could be incremental.

It could appear as a “sustained US-China strategic stability dialogue with concrete reciprocity – test moratoria, data exchanges [and] notification of major exercises”, he explained.

The negotiations would also need to address missile defence, advanced conventional weapons and emerging technologies, Sun said.

“Differentiated obligations and phased verification would offer a more workable basis than identical reductions,” he added.

Sun said a practical starting point would be to combine US-Russian arms negotiations with “three-way discussions on crisis communication, nuclear doctrines and human control over AI-enabled nuclear systems”.

Reyes said an agreement would have to accommodate different levels of nuclear capability rather than insist on identical ceilings because all three countries have different arsenals, strategic doctrines and security concerns.

“The fundamental obstacle is political trust,” he said. “Each side regards its own nuclear capabilities as defensive while viewing the others’ modernisation programmes as potentially threatening. That dynamic encourages an arms race even when no side necessarily wants one.”

Still, such a result may not emerge anytime soon with the Ukraine war, tensions over Taiwan and US military deployments in the Asia Pacific still sources of simmering conflict between Washington and Beijing, Zhao argued.

“The likeliest near-term outcome is not a treaty but informal restraints while formal arms control waits for a geopolitical thaw that this decade is unlikely to deliver,” Zhao added.

articles.title: 49ers offense puts up over 580 yards against a bad Cowboys defense behind a Christian McCaffrey masterclass
articles.excerpt: Dan reacts to CBS sideline reporter A.J. Ross revealing that Cleveland Browns head coach Todd Monken asked Shedeur Sanders which plays he liked for the opening drive against the Saints—and Sanders sug...
articles.body_text:
Dan reacts to CBS sideline reporter A.J. Ross revealing that Cleveland Browns head coach Todd Monken asked Shedeur Sanders which plays he liked for the opening drive against the Saints—and Sanders suggested plays that weren't even in Cleveland's playbook.

If there's a sole team above the rest in the NFL, it's the San Francisco 49ers.

San Francisco improved to 8-1 on Sunday with a 46-40 win at AT&T Stadium, piling up 584 total yards as red jerseys outnumbered and out-yelled home fans.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

It was a close battle until the third quarter when a pair of electric Niners rushing touchdowns stuffed the Cowboys in a deep hole.

CHRISTIAN MCCAFFREY GIVES ONE 49ERS QUALITY THAT SEPARATES TEAM FROM PACK AMID SUPER BOWL HOPES

Rookie Kaelon Black sparked the surge on the opening drive of the second half, lowering his shoulder to bulldoze two Cowboys defenders, including first-round pick Caleb Downs and cornerback Cobie Durant, on his way to a 25-yard scamper.

Moments later, the seasoned second-term Niners star, Deebo Samuel Sr., stuck the dagger in Dallas on a 70-yard reverse, taking a pitch from Black.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

On Sunday, San Francisco piled on 214 rushing yards: Black finished with 53 yards on 11 carries, while Samuel totaled 78 rushing yards on three carries in his first game back since Oct. 11, alongside an 11-yard touchdown catch.

Dak Prescott #4 of the Dallas Cowboys drops back to pass against the San Francisco 49ers during the second half of an NFL game at AT&T Stadium on Nov. 15, 2026, in Arlington, Texas. (Getty Images)

San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Deebo Samuel Sr. scores a touchdown against the Dallas Cowboys during the first quarter on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026, at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas. (TNS)

Christian McCaffrey added three touchdowns of his own, including 74- and 66-yard catch-and-runs, as the 49ers averaged more than 9 yards a play.

"Totally unacceptable defense," Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer said after the loss.

San Francisco's offensive clinic ruined a gutsy outing from Dak Prescott, who did everything possible to keep Dallas alive. Prescott threw for 343 yards and five touchdowns, hitting George Pickens three times in the end zone.

COWBOYS HIRE LONGTIME NFL COACH OUT OF RETIREMENT TO ADDRESS TEAM'S BRUTAL DEFENSIVE START

But Prescott's best efforts couldn't survive the defensive disaster led by first-year coordinator Christian Parker, who looked completely out of his depth as Kyle Shanahan picked Dallas apart for the most home yards allowed in franchise history.

Defensive coordinator Christian Parker of the Dallas Cowboys looks on during the third quarter of a game against the San Francisco 49ers at AT&T Stadium on Nov. 15, 2026, in Arlington, Texas. (Getty Images)
